title: Time, Ordering, Concurrency and Causality
results: Runtime has no universal single Time coordinate; physical time, wall/realtime clock, monotonic duration, logical order and causal order are distinct.
Wall timestamps are persistent/civil/evidence coordinates rather than universal duration proofs.
Monotonic clocks are the proper basis for local elapsed waits/deadlines; current Rust Instant use fits this role.
Occurrence time, observation time and record-commit time are distinct.
Lamport happened-before is a partial process/message/synchronization order rather than wall-clock order or complete physical causality.
Concurrency is incomparability under a declared order relation, not timestamp proximity alone.
Logical/total order can extend causal order without turning totalized pairs into causal relations.
Current event_sequence is a per-Job Registry append/serialization order rather than global physical chronology.
event_sequence and observed_at_ms are distinct order/time projections and may legitimately disagree.
Serializable concurrent operations may physically overlap while admitting a serial semantic explanation.
Linearizability adds preservation of real-time precedence for non-overlapping operations.
Current same-key races correctly rely on transactional admission serialization rather than caller-arrival order.
Temporal precedence, synchronization, lineage and causality are distinct.
Consistent distributed snapshots do not require simultaneous wall-clock reads.
External effect/receipt ordering remains effect-owner/protocol semantics absent a stronger clock/order contract.
Persisted Runtime latency measurements are useful wall/evidence diagnostics rather than exact monotonic/causal duration truth.
Partial/scoped order should be preserved by default and widened to total order only for explicit consumers.

nextRound.title: Authority, Capability, Permission and Control
nextRound.entryQuestion: Who or what can, may, authorizes, delegates and controls an Operation, and how do ability, identity, policy permission and authority differ across Runtime boundaries?

notes: RF5 explains Runtime clocks/order/concurrency semantics but does not authorize event schema, clock storage, timeout, global logical-clock or admission changes.
